Round 2 tried harder: checked whether PQShield publishes McEliece benchmarks (no match found in search — their public benchmarks appear focused on ML-KEM/ML-DSA/FN-DSA, not Classic McEliece); attempted direct fetches of the three most likely primary sources — the NIST Chou 2022 presentation PDF, the official Classic McEliece implementation guide (classic.mceliece.org/mceliece-impl-20221023.pdf), and an academic PQC performance survey (arXiv:2204.02571) — all three failed to yield an extractable table (PDF parsing errors or the number data is embedded in images/compressed streams the fetch tool cannot read). use_case_notes: RECONCILED 2026-07-06 (previously flagged as contradicting the Learn module's framing of LAC as "continued as a domestic Chinese reference design" — see PQCCandidates/data/nationalCandidates.ts). Web research confirms: LAC (Lu, Liu, Jia, Xue, He — DACAS/Chinese Academy of Sciences) won CACR's national PQC algorithm design competition as "LAC.KEX" (~2018-2020) — that part of the Learn module claim is accurate. Separately, LAC was submitted to NIST PQC as a Round 2 KEM candidate and was NOT advanced to Round 3; documented concerns included non-constant-time implementations of its error-correction-based decryption-failure-fixing routine (a side-channel risk). NO EVIDENCE FOUND of LAC/LAC.KEX being subsequently adopted as an actual OSCCA/GB Chinese national cryptographic standard — winning a design competition is not the same as national standardization, and this project found nothing indicating production deployment. China's current forward-looking PQC standardization effort is the separate, newer NGCC program (2025-2028; see NGCC-BC/NGCC-CH rows and the timeline CSV), reported to be leaning toward newer "structureless lattice" designs (e.g. S-Cloud+) rather than continuing LAC. Sizes/cycles still unconfirmed — some sources estimate ~352 B (pk/ct) but this project has not verified them against a primary CACR document; left as Research needed. use_case_notes: ETSI-standardised hybrid attribute-based KEM with access control (KEMAC). Combines a classical KEM (ECIES) with a post-quantum KEM (ML-KEM) and enforces attribute-based access policies at the key layer. Sizes are inherently VARIABLE / policy-dependent — they scale with the complexity of the access policy, not just the KEM parameter set. The reference document (pqctoday-priv/docs/PQC_Algorithm_Reference_April2026.csv) confirms this and does not give concrete byte counts. Active deployments use Cosmian's reference implementation. ETSI TS 104 015 published Feb 2025.

"HPKE-PQ" is NOT a single concrete algorithm — it is HPKE (RFC 9180) configured with a PQ KEM. Sizes shown are for the most common mode HPKE-PQ (ML-KEM-768): pk=1184 B, ct=1088 B, shared secret=32 B. Cycle figures approximate ML-KEM-768's own cost (1.5x, already on this table's PQC baseline) since HPKE's KDF (HKDF)+AEAD wrapper overhead is small relative to the KEM operation itself (single-digit-percent, per RFC 9180's own performance discussion) and does not materially change the ratio at this precision — an approximation, not a direct benchmark of HPKE-PQ itself. The HPKE framework wraps a KEM, a KDF, and an AEAD; concrete costs vary with the chosen KEM/AEAD. IETF Internet-Draft draft-ietf-hpke-pq-03 (active, expires May 2026). Used by MLS messaging, Encrypted Client Hello (ECH), and Oblivious HTTP. Verified against pqctoday-priv/docs/PQC_Algorithm_Reference_April2026.csv.

use_case_notes: Classic McEliece alternate Level 5 parameter set (mceliece6960119). pk=1,047,319 / sk=13,948 / ct=194 per pqctoday-priv/docs/PQC_Algorithm_Reference_April2026.csv (sizes confirmed via OQS reference implementation). BSI-recommended (alongside -6688128) as a conservative ~256-bit-equivalent option for long-term sovereign protection. Distinct from -6688128 (pk=1,044,992, ct=208) and -8192128 (pk=1,357,824, ct=208) — same security level, different code parameters. NIST did not select Classic McEliece in the Fourth Round (NIST IR 8545, 2025-03-11; HQC selected instead). Cycle benchmarks not yet recorded here. CYCLE RESEARCH ATTEMPTED 2026-07-06 (two rounds): round 1 found self-contradictory search-tool synthesis (the same figure attributed to different operations across queries). Round 2 tried harder: checked whether PQShield publishes McEliece benchmarks (no match found in search — their public benchmarks appear focused on ML-KEM/ML-DSA/FN-DSA, not Classic McEliece); attempted direct fetches of the three most likely primary sources — the NIST Chou 2022 presentation PDF, the official Classic McEliece implementation guide (classic.mceliece.org/mceliece-impl-20221023.pdf), and an academic PQC performance survey (arXiv:2204.02571) — all three failed to yield an extractable table (PDF parsing errors or the number data is embedded in images/compressed streams the fetch tool cannot read). A follow-up search then produced a THIRD set of numbers that disagreed with both prior rounds by 2-5x and did not preserve consistent relative ordering between the two parameter sets — reinforcing that automated search synthesis is not reliable for this specific figure. Left as Research needed rather than pick one of the disagreeing numbers. A human with direct PDF/browser access should open mceliece-impl-20221023.pdf directly and read the benchmark table by eye, or check bench.cr.yp.to's per-machine Haswell/Skylake results page linked from https://bench.cr.yp.to/results-kem.html.

General-purpose hybrid KEM combining X25519 and ML-KEM-768; unlike the TLS named groups it is not bound to any one protocol, and is used for file and secrets encryption (age / SOPS) as well as on the wire. Sizes quoted verbatim from draft-connolly-cfrg-xwing-kem-10 section 5.1: decapsulation key 32 bytes (seed), encapsulation key 1216 bytes, ciphertext 1120 bytes, shared secret 32 bytes. Inherits NIST security level 3 from ML-KEM-768.

SSH transport hybrid key exchange combining Streamlined NTRU Prime sntrup761 with X25519; OpenSSH's default since 9.x and offered by our own OpenSSH build. RFC 9941 states the sizes directly: Q_C is the 1158-byte sntrup761 public key concatenated with the 32-byte X25519 share (1190 bytes), and 'The Q_S value is thus 1071 bytes' (1039-byte sntrup761 ciphertext + 32). Shared secret is the SHA-512 output, 64 bytes. NOTE: sntrup761 is a NIST round-3 alternate, not a FIPS-standardised algorithm, so this hybrid carries no NIST security level.

SSH transport hybrid key exchange per draft-ietf-sshm-mlkem-hybrid-kex-10: the client sends C_INIT = C_PK2 || C_PK1 and the server S_REPLY = S_CT2 || S_PK1, with the shared secret K = HASH(K_PQ || K_CL). Sizes DERIVED by concatenation from this catalogue's own component rows (ML-KEM-768 1184/1088 + X25519 32); the draft itself states no byte counts. Shared secret is the SHA-256 output, 32 bytes. Offered by our own OpenSSH build alongside sntrup761x25519-sha512.

use_case_notes: Schnorr signature over Ristretto-compressed Curve25519 (Schnorrkel); default account-signing scheme for Polkadot/Substrate chains; dual-purpose like Ed25519 in Solana, also used for BABE consensus (VRF + block signing); supports native key aggregation/multisig and hierarchical derivation (HDKD) that Ed25519 lacks; not an IETF/NIST standard, no FIPS mapping; vulnerable to quantum attacks on the discrete-log problem like all classical ECC

fips_standard: GB/T 32918 (China); ISO/IEC 14888-3:2018; NOT in NIST FIPS
use_case_notes: Chinese national ('ShangMi') elliptic-curve signature algorithm over a 256-bit prime field; mandatory in China for commercial cryptography. Standardized internationally in ISO/IEC 14888-3:2018 and profiled for TLS 1.3 (RFC 8998) and DNSSEC (RFC 9563, algorithm number 17). Byte sizes verified against RFC 9563: 64-byte uncompressed public key (x||y), 64-byte signature (r||s, 32 bytes each); vulnerable to quantum attacks like all classical ECC.
